steps.title: Three levels
steps.body: The Vinea Wachau, a growers' association founded in 1983, created three categories for dry wines. Steinfeder, named after a feather grass, is light, up to 11.5% alcohol. Federspiel, named after a falconry lure, is medium, 11.5 to 12.5%. Smaragd, named after an emerald-green lizard, is the ripest, above 12.5%.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body: All three are dry, made only from Wachau grapes, without chaptalisation or concentration. Smaragd comes from the ripest grapes, often from top terraces, and can age 10 to 20 years. Unlike Germany's Prädikat, which measures sugar at harvest, these categories reflect alcohol in the finished dry wine.

steps.prompt: Order the Wachau categories from lightest to fullest.
steps.explanation: Riper grapes from the best sites give the fullest wines.

steps.title: Wachau DAC
steps.body: In 2020, the Wachau became a DAC, with three levels of origin: Gebietswein, regional; Ortswein, village; and Riedenwein, single vineyard, with Ried on the label. The Vinea Wachau categories continue alongside. Labels may show both, like Ried Achleiten Riesling Smaragd.

steps.explanation: The lizard basks on the terraces in the sun.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd grade dry wines by alcohol
Smaragd is the ripest and can age 10 to 20 years
Wachau DAC, since 2020, adds village and vineyard levels
